{{short description|19th-century Scottish mathematician}}
{{about||the British Army officer|Thomas James Galloway|the British politician|Thomas Galbraith, 2nd Baron Strathclyde|the engineer and author|T. Lindsay Galloway}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2021}}
'''Thomas Galloway''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (26 February 1796{{snd}}1 November 1851) was a 19th-century [[Scotland|Scottish]] [[mathematician]].

==Life==

He was born in [[Symington, South Lanarkshire]], [[Scotland]]. In 1812 he entered the [[University of Edinburgh]], where he distinguished himself in mathematics. In 1823 he was appointed one of the teachers of mathematics at the [[Royal Military College, Sandhurst]], and in 1833 he became an [[actuary]] of the Amicable Life Assurance Office, the oldest institution of that kind in London, where he remained until his death in 1851. Galloway was a voluminous, though, for the most part, anonymous writer. His most notable paper, "On the proper motion of the solar system", was published in the ''Philosophical Transactions'' of 1847. He contributed largely to the seventh edition of [[Encyclopædia Britannica]], and also wrote several scientific papers for the ''Edinburgh Review'' and various scientific journals. His ''Encyclopaedia'' article, "Probability", was published separately.<ref>{{EB1911|inline=y|wstitle=Galloway, Thomas|volume=11|page=422}}</ref> He is buried in [[Kensal Green Cemetery]], London.

==Family==

Galloway married a daughter of the mathematician [[William Wallace (mathematician)|William Wallace]],<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Case of Mary Somerville: An Aspect of Nineteenth-Century Science|first=Elizabeth C.|last=Patterson|journal=Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society|date=June 7, 1974|volume=118|issue=3|pages=269–275|jstor=986445}} See footnote 23, p. 271.</ref> in 1831.<ref>{{cite DNB|wstitle=Galloway, Thomas |short=x}}</ref>
